'''Stacey R. Smith?'''{{efn|Her personal website says the question mark is part of her name,<ref>{{cite web |first=Stacey |last=Smith? |url=https://rsmith43.github.io/mysite/ |title=Welcome to the homepage of Stacey Smith? |website=[[University of Ottawa]] |access-date=February 24, 2025}}</ref> and at some point she also added a question mark at the end of her former name.<ref name=CBCBieberFever/><!-- The CBC source explicitly says the name did not originally include a question mark but was changed to add it. --><ref name=mathgenealogy/><ref name=ForeignPolicy/>}} (formerly '''Robert Joseph Smith?''',<ref name=mathgenealogy/><ref name=ForeignPolicy>{{cite news |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2015/08/23/which-country-is-best-prepared-for-the-zombie-apocalypse-fear-the-walking-dead/ |last=Standish |first=Reid |title=Which Country Is Best Prepared for the Zombie Apocalypse? |website=[[Foreign Policy]] |date=August 23, 2015}}</ref> born 28 October 1972) is an Australian-Canadian mathematician known for scholarly research work on the modeling of infectious outbreaks, particularly including the analysis of outbreaks of [[zombies]] and [[Bieber Fever]] (a phenomenon characterized by extreme fandom for the Canadian singer [[Justin Bieber]]). She has also published scholarly books on [[science fiction]].

==Life and career==
Smith? received a bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Macquarie University]] in Sydney, Australia, in 1994. After graduation, she went to [[McMaster University]], where she received a master's degree in 1996 and a Ph.D. in 2001. Her doctoral thesis investigated the technique of self-cycling fermentation; her Ph.D. advisor was [[Gail Wolkowicz]].<ref name=mathgenealogy>{{mathgenealogy|68340|title=Robert Joseph Smith?}}</ref>

After finishing her doctorate, Smith? worked as a [[postdoctoral researcher]] at the [[University of Western Ontario]], where she became involved with the mathematical study of disease. Smith? did further postdoctoral research at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], and at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]].

In 2009, Smith? published the first academic article mathematically modeling a [[zombie]] outbreak, which brought Smith? to the attention of international media,<ref name=NBCSurviving>{{cite news|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna52625389|work=NBC News|title=Surviving a Zombie Apocalypse: Just Do the Math|first=Michael|last=Dhar|date=July 30, 2013|access-date=2024-12-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2009-08-18 |title=Science ponders 'zombie attack' |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/8206280.stm |access-date=2026-03-16 |work=[[BBC]] |language=en-GB}}</ref> including a [[Guinness World Record]] for being the first mathematician to create such a model.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/first-mathematical-model-for-surviving-a-zombie-attack|title=First mathematical model for surviving a zombie attack|work=Guinness World Records|access-date=2024-12-29}}</ref> Smith? received further attention in media in 2012 for publishing a mathematical model of "[[Bieber Fever]]", together with her student, Valerie Tweedle.<ref name=CBCBieberFever>{{cite news|title='Bieber Fever' more infectious than measles|agency=[[The Canadian Press]] |website=[[Canadian Broadcasting Company]]|date=June 7, 2012|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/bieber-fever-more-infectious-than-measles-1.1236221|access-date=2024-12-29}}</ref><ref name=TorontoSunBieberFever>{{cite news|newspaper=[[The Toronto Sun]] |agency=[[QMI Agency]] |url=https://torontosun.com/2012/06/07/bieber-fever-an-infectious-disease-study|title=Bieber Fever an infectious disease: Study|date=June 7, 2012|access-date=2024-12-29}}</ref> In 2019, she was awarded the [[Society for Mathematical Biology]]'s Distinguished Service Award, and then elected a fellow of the Society in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Distinguished Service Award |url=https://www.smb.org/distinguished-service-award/ |access-date=2025-02-24 |website=Society for Mathematical Biology}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Society for Mathematical Biology Fellows |url=https://www.smb.org/Society-for-Mathematical-Biology-Fellows |access-date=2025-02-24 |website=Society for Mathematical Biology}}</ref>

As of December 2025, Smith? is a professor of mathematics and statistics at the [[University of Ottawa]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uottawa.ca/faculty-science/professors/stacey-smith|title=Stacey Smith?|work=Faculty of Science professors|publisher=University of Ottawa|access-date=2024-08-18}}</ref>

She has also written a ''[[Doctor Who]]'' short story published in the "Short Trips: History of Christmas" collection, as well as several ''Doctor Who'' reference books.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-05 |title=Welcoming Author Stacy Smith? to Our 2023 Con |url=https://www.chicagotardis.com/ctupdatearchive/welcomingstacysmith2023 |access-date=2025-12-07 |website=Chicago TARDIS |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Smith? is a [[trans woman]] and is [[polyamory|polyamorous]].<ref>{{cite podcast |first=Amanda |last=Pfeffer |title=Why Does Polyamory Work for You? |url=https://www.cbc.ca/listen/live-radio/1-45-ontario-today/clip/16071119-why-polyamory-work-you |website=Ontario Today with Amanda Pfeffer |publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]}}</ref>
